catalog_citation: Boyd, Raymond. 1999. A Linguistic Sketch of Tiba (Gà). Afrika und Übersee 82: 1-17 (Part I), 213-249 (Part II). Author's corrected Unicode version of both parts, HAL hal-00323718v3 (65 pp.).
catalog_locator: Part II, §II.1 'Tiba phonology', subsection d) TONES; HAL pp. 31-32 (the tone-system paragraph and downstep paragraph on p. 31, 'NOUN TONE CLASSES' at the top of p. 32). Printed in Afrika und Übersee 82: 213-249; the HAL version carries no printed pagination.
catalog_quote: d) TONES Tiba has a three-level tone system, complicated by downstep and grammatical tone alternation. Downstep occurs automatically (as a mere phonetic realization) after a rising (LH) contour tone. It also occurs syntactically (i.e., as a mark of certain syntactic relationships without necessarily requiring postulation of any "underlying" (deleted) L tone), and as a "surface" phenomenon, i.e., where the deletion of an underlying tone may be supposed. Within lexical units, this underlying tone may be structurally L; but the most frequent deletion affects HM contour tones and patterns ... This situation, resulting from the abundance of such tones and patterns in nominal lexical units (see below), is largely identical to the one in CD. ... NOUN TONE CLASSES: Note that about one half of all nominals have a HM or H tone pattern; another quarter has MH or M. Other fairly well represented nominal root tone patterns are LH, LHM, HL(M), and L. The others are marginal and perhaps derivable in some way from the above.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

The second half of the bridged quote ('NOUN TONE CLASSES: Note that about one half of all nominals have a HM or H tone pattern; another quarter has MH or M. Other fairly well represented nominal root tone patterns are LH, LHM, HL(M), and L.') is verbatim but sits at the top of p. 32, not p. 31 -- the only discrepancy with the stated locator. Section is II.1 'Tiba phonol…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The language is described as a three-level (H, M, L) tone language with downstep and grammatical tone alternation; lexical tone patterns are listed for nouns and verbs. The words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur in a phonological sense anywhere in the 65-page sketch.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (none stated). For tone: downstep after LH contours; H/HM nouns change tone when modified; verb tone classes hard to establish from the elicitation context.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone (nouns, verbs) plus syntactic downstep; data from one informant, elicited via Chamba Daka (the author calls the description provisional).
new_statements.identity_note: Boyd 1999 describes 'Tiba (Gà)' from one speaker at Gambe near Pola, Adamawa State, Nigeria; autonym per Boyd 'Gà(ã)'; this is the gaaa1245 language (Glottolog, PHOIBLE and Grambank all attach Boyd 1999 to gaaa1245). Boyd argues it is Adamawa (Mumuye-Yendang) heavily relexified from Chamba Daka, against the Ethnologue/Glottolog Dakoid placement. The Glottolog ref Djouonzo 2005 'Nom en Təbaya (Tiba)' is a Yaoundé thesis on Tibea (tibe1274, Cameroon) and almost certainly not this language.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement from Boyd 1999 (three-level tone system; no stress statement). Adds contour-tone detail (HL/ML/HM/MH/LH on single vowels; HM/HL/MH/LM/LH/LHM on doubled vowels) and confirms the identification Gãã = Tiba, ISO ttb, gaaa1245. Confidence medium only because the text read is Academia's extraction of the slides, not the PDF; the slide text is complete (35 slides) but table cells are flattened.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gãã (Tiba) has three contrastive tone heights (H, M, L) plus contour tones on single vowels (HL, ML, HM, MH, LH) and on doubled vowels; tone is lexically and morphologically contrastive. Nothing is said about word stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the slide text (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence: the only hit is 'the most prominent of these [verb suffixes] is -si', not phonological).
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; on tone the slides note that a velar nasal standing alone bears a tone but as a velar release bears none, and that contour tones on single vowels probably arose from shortening of doubled vowels
new_statements.identity_note: Blench 2025 describes Gãã as spoken on the Shebshi Plateau, Adamawa and Taraba States, Nigeria, data from two speakers (Hammanjoda Yakitiso, Usman Sementakari) working in Jos in 2025, ~1400 lemmas; it explicitly gives ISO ttb and Glottocode gaaa1245 and equates Gãã with Tiba. No dialect is singled out. ( also notes that the Glottolog-listed Djouonzo 2005 'Nom en Təbaya (Tiba)' is a Cameroonian thesis matched to tibe1274 Tibea, almost certainly a different 'Tiba'; it was not in this task's works list.)

tone_statements.quote: The tones are written as heard, pending more nuanced analysis. ... 2.3 Tones Gãã has three contrastive tone heights, as shown in Table 3; ... Table 3.
